messages.subject: memory usage, wiener first passage time distribution, rstan, windows
parts:
Hello,

when doing a parameter recovery experiment to test the new wiener distribution function in stan (thanks for adding it!),
I find that I can't fit meaningful amounts of data because under some circumstances memory is quickly exhausted.

Before describing the problem in detail I will say that model recovery works well when I use (simulated) data that are small enough!

The problem occurs on my desktop with only 8GB RAM, but I assume the same will happen with meaning full amounts of data on machines with more RAM.

In particular, I am observing a large variability in memory usage when sampling for a new chain starts:
The RAM usage increase varies between not noticeable and around 2.5GB .
The attached figure illustrates this for example data (also attached). 
While in this example the large increase in RAM usage happens for the first chain,
I found that this can also happen for later chains (with different data or seeds).

My question is if this could have anything to do with the initialization, such more memory is used when starting values for parameters are bad?
One indication for this is that much less RAM is used when I initialize sampling with plausible parameter values.
Even if bad initial values are the culprit, I would be curious as to if the amount of memory usage is expected in that case.

Another (undesirable) behavior I observed is that the memory used is not released after sampling is done.
That is, even though the returned stanfit object has only around 0.35 MB. The RAM usage stays at the maximum
reached during sampling.

I am also getting the following warning, which I assume can be ignored.
Warning (non-fatal):
 Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If so, you need to call increment_log_prob() with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
    segment(RTu,posu,get_base1(su,k,"su",1)) ~ wiener(...)

After checking the user-list I assume that I can ignore the warning, but I am not sure.

The attached files should allow to reproduce the observed behavior:

Thanks in advance!

Guido

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] memory usage, wiener first passage time distribution, rstan, windows
parts:
Another quick thought on the possible memory leak issue; sometimes simply looking at an OS's memory monitor isn't an accurate gauge of the memory status as the OS will often show memory being allocated even when released if no new data allocations have been requested since the release. The true test is to try to allocate a new object and see if you encounter an unexpected out of memory error or paging to disk.


--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] memory usage, wiener first passage time distribution, rstan, windows
parts:
It's not initialization/warmup that's the issue. There's no
major difference in memory usage for the Stan infrastructure itself
between inits in the typical set or far out into the tails.

The most likely cause is an iterative algorithm that is being
autodiffed through that takes more iteration in the tails than in
the typical set. We see this with the ODE integrator, for example.

Do you know what values the function's being called with that eat
lots of memory?

I don't know anything about how R recovers memory, but Stan itself
recovers (or should recover) all memory after each log density
evaluation (each leapfrog step in HMC or NUTS).

- Bob

parts:
Here are examples for "good" and "bad" initialisation values, where "bad" means that lots of RAM is consumed when using these values.
I replicated the issue on a mac now, so it is  not windows specific.

For the example below I found that fitting with bad initialisation values lead to a consumption of around 3800mb, whereas good initialisation values used around 900mb. At first I thought that the problem could be caused by inits close to the boundaries of constrained parameters. but I am not sure.

To replicate my results on a mac you can do the following in R (session info at the end of the email):

load("wiener_test_data.Rdata") # data attached to the first mail in this thread
m = stan_model(file = "stan_wiener_test2.stan") # stan file attached to the first mail in this thread

bad_inits = list(delta = c(-0.7987087, 1.302651, 0.420765, 0.2789249),
                 alpha = c(1.271243, 7.667402, 1.437398, 2.138264),
                 beta  = c(0.4081320, 0.5393007, 0.7897648, 0.8449466),
                 tau   = c(0.1105052, 0.1264254, 0.1413274, 0.1196919))


get_mem = function() {as.numeric(sub("M","",strsplit(system("top -l 1 | head -n 10 | grep PhysMem",intern = T)," ")[[1]][2]))}


mem_before_fit = get_mem()
fit_inits = sampling(m,data = stan_data,iter = 400,seed = 1234,
                     chains = 1, init = list(bad_inits))
consumed_memory = get_mem()-mem_before_fit
consumed_memory

then close the R session, open a new session (or simply Session-> Restart R in RStudio)
and repeat the code above with good initialisation inits:

good_inits = list(delta = c(0, 0, 0, 0),
                  beta  = c(.5, .5, .5, .5),
                  alpha = c(1, 1, 1, 1),
                  tau   = c(.11, .11, .11, .11))



Guido

parts:
Thanks for following up.

That's not unexpected --- there's an underlying iterative algorithm
and we're autodiffing through it, which means the memory is going to
be proportional to the number of iterations run. You might be able
to mitigate some of that problem by starting with a smaller initial
step size. Now if we could get analytic gradients, the memory wouldn't
be so bad. So if anyone knows how to do that (even if the gradients
themselves are an iterative algorithm), it'd really help.

We've been doing that gradually with matrix operations and distributions.
The next release is going to hugely reduce the memory required to do
a Cholesky factorization, for example.

- Bob
